chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: The history of Spain dates to contact between the pre-Roman peoples of the Mediterranean coast of the Iberian Peninsula with the Greeks and Phoenicians. During Classical Antiquity, the peninsula was the site of multiple successive colonizations of Greeks, Carthaginians, and Romans.

events.text: Germanic control lasted until the Umayyad conquest of Hispania began in 711.
The early modern period is generally dated from the union of the Crowns of Castile and Aragon by royal marriage in 1469.
The conquest of Granada, and the first voyage of Columbus, both in 1492, made that year a critical inflection point in Spanish history.
During the re-establishment of the Bourbon rule in Spain, constitutional monarchy was introduced in 1813.
Concurrent with, and following, the Napoleonic period the Spanish American wars of independence resulted in the loss of most of Spain's territory in the Americas in the 1820s.
A new liberal Constitution was established in 1978.
Spain entered the European Economic Community in 1986 (transformed into the European Union in 1992), and the Eurozone in 1998.
Juan Carlos abdicated in 2014, and was succeeded by his son Felipe VI.

chapters.narrative: History of Spain dates to contact between pre-Roman peoples of the Mediterranean coast of the Iberian Peninsula with Greeks and Phoenicians [S1]. During Classical Antiquity the peninsula was site of successive colonizations of Greeks, Carthaginians, and Romans [S1]. Germanic control lasted until Umayyad conquest began in 711 [S1]. Early modern period is dated from union of Crowns of Castile and Aragon in 1469, with conquest of Granada and first voyage of Columbus in 1492 as critical inflection point [S1]. Constitutional monarchy was introduced in 1813, and Spanish American wars after Napoleonic period led to loss of most American territory in 1820s [S1]. New liberal Constitution was established in 1978 [S1]. Spain entered European Economic Community in 1986 and Eurozone in 1998, and Juan Carlos abdicated in 2014 succeeded by Felipe VI [S1].

chapters.title: Prehistory
chapters.summary: The earliest record of Homo genus representatives living in Western Europe has been found in the Spanish cave of Atapuerca; a flint tool found there dates from 1.4 million years ago, and early human fossils date to roughly 1.2 million years ago. The Iberian Peninsula was one of the last regions of Europe where Neanderthals persisted during the expansion of modern humans, with Neanderthal populations surviving in parts of Iberia until around 40,000 years ago.

events.label: 2500 BC
events.text: Around 2500–2000 BC, the immigration of Bell Beaker-associated populations carrying Steppe ancestry into the Iberian Peninsula was accompanied by the replacement of about 40% of the ancestry of the earlier Neolithic population and nearly all of its Y-chromosome lineages, with the latter predominantly replaced by R1b lineages, which remain the predominant Y-chromosome lineage among present-day Spanish populations.

chapters.narrative: The earliest record of Homo genus representatives living in Western Europe has been found in the Spanish cave of Atapuerca, where a flint tool dates from 1.4 million years ago and early human fossils date to roughly 1.2 million years ago [S2]. The Iberian Peninsula was one of the last regions of Europe where Neanderthals persisted during the expansion of modern humans, with Neanderthal populations surviving in parts of Iberia until around 40,000 years ago [S2]. Around 2500–2000 BC, immigration of Bell Beaker-associated populations carrying Steppe ancestry into the Iberian Peninsula was accompanied by replacement of about 40% of the ancestry of the earlier Neolithic population and nearly all of its Y-chromosome lineages, predominantly replaced by R1b lineages [S2]. These R1b lineages remain the predominant Y-chromosome lineage among present-day Spanish populations [S2].

chapters.title: Early history of the Iberian Peninsula
chapters.summary: Before the Roman conquest the major cultures along the Mediterranean coast were the Iberians, the Celts in the interior and north-west, the Lusitanians in the west, and the Tartessians in the southwest. The seafaring Phoenicians, Carthaginians, and Greeks successively established trading settlements along the eastern and southern coast.

events.label: 9th c. BC
events.text: The development of writing in the peninsula took place after the arrival of early Phoenician settlers and traders (tentatively dated 9th century BC or later).

events.label: 7th c. BC
events.text: Archaic Greeks arrived on the Peninsula by the late 7th century BC.

events.label: 570 BC
events.text: They founded Greek colonies such as Emporion (570 BC).

events.label: 6th c. BC
events.text: By the 6th century BC, much of the territory of southern Iberia passed to Carthage's overarching influence (featuring two centres of Punic influence in Gadir and Mastia); the latter grip strengthened from the 4th century BC on.

events.label: 237 BC
events.text: The Barcids, following their landing in Gadir in 237 BC, conquered the territories that belonged to the sphere of influence of Carthage.

events.label: 219 BC
events.text: Until 219 BC, their presence in the peninsula was underpinned by their control of places such as Carthago Nova and Akra Leuké (both founded by Punics), as well as the network of old Phoenician settlements.

events.label: 218 BC
events.text: The peninsula was a military theatre of the Second Punic War (218–201 BC) waged between Carthage and the Roman Republic, the two powers vying for supremacy in the western Mediterranean.

events.label: 206 BC
events.text: Romans expelled Carthaginians from the peninsula in 206 BC.

events.label: 181 BC
events.text: The Celtiberian Wars were fought between the advancing legions of the Roman Republic and the Celtiberian tribes of Hispania Citerior from 181 to 133 BC.

chapters.narrative: Before the Roman conquest the major cultures along the Mediterranean coast were the Iberians, the Celts in the interior and north-west, the Lusitanians in the west, and the Tartessians in the southwest [S3]. The seafaring Phoenicians, Carthaginians, and Greeks successively established trading settlements along the eastern and southern coast [S3]. The development of writing in the peninsula took place after the arrival of early Phoenician settlers and traders (tentatively dated 9th century BC or later) [S3]. Archaic Greeks arrived on the Peninsula by the late 7th century BC and founded Greek colonies such as Emporion (570 BC) [S3]. By the 6th century BC, much of the territory of southern Iberia passed to Carthage's overarching influence [S3]. The peninsula was a military theatre of the Second Punic War (218–201 BC) waged between Carthage and the Roman Republic [S3]. Romans expelled Carthaginians from the peninsula in 206 BC [S3].

chapters.title: Roman Hispania (2nd century BC – 5th century AD)
chapters.summary: Hispania was the name used for the Iberian Peninsula under Roman rule from the 2nd century BC. The population was gradually culturally Romanized, and local leaders were admitted into the Roman aristocratic class.

events.label: 2nd c. BC
events.text: Hispania was the name used for the Iberian Peninsula under Roman rule from the 2nd century BC.

events.label: 3rd c.
events.text: In the 3rd century, the Roman Empire experienced a severe crisis.

events.label: 4th c.
events.text: Under the Dominate and Tetrarchy in the 4th century, peace returned, and the provinces recovered from the damage sustained.
In 395, the Empire was divided in two, and Spain was added to the Western Roman Empire.
In 405/406, following the Rhine crossing, various barbarian tribes entered the empire and caused chaos.

events.label: 5th c.
events.text: It was a harbinger of what awaited the empire in the 5th century.

Under the Dominate and Tetrarchy in the 4th century, peace returned, and the provinces recovered from the damage sustained [S4]. These excerpts reflect only a Roman imperial point of view [S4].

chapters.title: Visigothic Hispania (5th–8th centuries)
chapters.summary: The first Barbarian tribes to invade Hispania arrived in 409 from Gaul The Suebi, Vandals and Alans arrived by crossing the Pyrenees mountain range, leading to the establishment of the Suebi Kingdom in Gallaecia, in the northwest and the Vandal Kingdom of Vandalusia (Andalusia). Their influence increased rapidly because the Roman army had been largely withdrawn from Spain due to the civil war.

events.text: The first Barbarian tribes to invade Hispania arrived in 409 from Gaul The Suebi, Vandals and Alans arrived by crossing the Pyrenees mountain range, leading to the establishment of the Suebi Kingdom in Gallaecia, in the northwest and the Vandal Kingdom of Vandalusia (Andalusia).
The Visigoths arrived in Gaul in 412, where they received land from the Romans in Aquitania in exchange for military help.
After their loss against the Franks in battle of Vouillé (507) the Visigoths shifted their capital to Toledo and reached a high point during the reign of Liuvigild.
The new quest age debated creed and liturgy in orthodox Catholicism, and the Council of Lerida in 546 constrained the clergy and extended the power of law over them with the approval of the Pope.
In 587, the Visigothic king at Toledo, Reccared, converted to Catholicism and launched a movement to unify the various religious doctrines in Hispania.

events.label: 7th c.
events.text: The  Visigothic crypt (the Crypt of San Antolín) in the Palencia Cathedral is a Visigothic chapel from the mid 7th century, built during the reign of Wamba to preserve the remains of the martyr Saint Antoninus of Pamiers.
The Liber Iudiciorum or Lex Visigothorum (654), also known as the Book of Judges, which Recceswinth promulgated, based on Roman law and Germanic customary laws, brought about legal unification.

events.label: 8th c.
events.text: The Visigothic Kingdom conquered all of Hispania and ruled it until the early 8th century, when the peninsula fell to the Muslim conquests.
Suintila's crown was stolen in 1921 and never recovered.

chapters.title: Islamic al-Andalus and the Christian Reconquest (8th–15th centuries)
chapters.summary: In 711 an Islamic Berber conquering party, led by Tariq ibn Ziyad, was sent to Hispania to intervene in a civil war in the Visigothic Kingdom. Crossing the Strait of Gibraltar, they won a decisive victory in the summer of 711 when the Visigothic King Roderic was defeated and killed on July 19 at the Battle of Guadalete.

events.text: In 711 an Islamic Berber conquering party, led by Tariq ibn Ziyad, was sent to Hispania to intervene in a civil war in the Visigothic Kingdom.
In 739, a rebellion in Galicia, assisted by the Asturians, drove out Muslim forces and it joined the Asturian kingdom.

events.label: 10th c.
events.text: In the 10th century Abd-al-Rahman III declared the Caliphate of Córdoba, effectively breaking all ties with the Egyptian and Syrian caliphs.
After the loss of Toledo in 1085, the Muslim rulers reluctantly invited the Almoravids, who invaded Al-Andalus from North Africa and established an empire.

events.label: 12th c.
events.text: In the 12th century the Almoravid empire broke up again, only to be taken over by the Almohad invasion, who were defeated by an alliance of the Christian kingdoms in the decisive Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
Spanish imperial conquest and colonization began with the Canary Islands in 1312 and 1402. which began the Castilian conquest of the Canary Islands, completed in 1495.
The Castilian conquest of the Canary Islands, inhabited by Guanche people, took place between 1402 (with the conquest of Lanzarote) and 1496 (with the conquest of Tenerife).

events.label: 15th c.
events.text: In the 15th century, the most important among all of the Christian kingdoms that made up the old Hispania were the Kingdom of Castile, the Kingdom of Aragon, and the Kingdom of Portugal.

When Spain's first Habsburg ruler Charles I became king of Spain in 1516 (with his mother and co-monarch Queen Juana I effectively powerless and kept imprisoned till her death in 1555), Spain became central to the dynastic struggles of Europe.

From the incorporation of the Portuguese Empire in 1580 (lost in 1640) until the loss of its American colonies in the 19th century, Spain maintained one of the largest empires in the world even though it suffered military and economic misfortunes from the 1640s.

chapters.narrative: In 711 an Islamic Berber conquering party, led by Tariq ibn Ziyad, was sent to Hispania to intervene in a civil war in the Visigothic Kingdom, where King Roderic was defeated and killed on July 19 at the Battle of Guadalete [S6]. In the 10th century Abd-al-Rahman III declared the Caliphate of Córdoba, breaking ties with the Egyptian and Syrian caliphs [S6]. After the loss of Toledo in 1085, Muslim rulers invited the Almoravids who invaded from North Africa, later replaced by the Almohads who were defeated in 1212 at Las Navas de Tolosa [S6]. The Canary Islands, inhabited by Guanche people, were conquered by Castile between 1402 and 1496 [S6]. The excerpts reflect mainly a political-military viewpoint focused on rulers and conquests [S6].

chapters.title: Spain under the Bourbons, 1715–1808
chapters.summary: Charles II died in 1700, and having no direct heir, was succeeded by his great-nephew Philip, Duke of Anjou, a French prince. The War of the Spanish Succession (1700–1714) pitted proponents of the Bourbon succession against those for the Habsburg.

events.text: Fearing that Britain's victory over France in the Seven Years' War (1756–63) threatened the European balance of power, Spain allied itself to France and invaded Portugal, a British ally, but suffered a series of military defeats and ended up having to cede Florida to the British at the Treaty of Paris (1763) while gaining Louisiana from France.
He had served as Prime Minister under King Charles III from 1777 until 1792; However, he tended to be suspicious of the popular spontaneity and resisted a revolution.
Spain regained Florida with the Treaty of Paris (1783), which ended the American Revolutionary War (1775–83), and gained an improved international standing.
Spain was at war with Britain 1798–1808, and the British blockade cut Spain's ties to the overseas empire.
A major Franco-Spanish fleet was lost at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, prompting the king to reconsider his difficult alliance with Napoleon.

Spain was put under a British blockade, and her colonies began to trade independently with Britain, but Britain invaded and was defeated in the British invasions of the Río de la Plata in South America (1806 and 1807) without help from mainland Spain, which emboldened independence and revolutionary hopes in Spain's American colonies.

Charles IV's vacillation, culminating in his failure to honour the alliance by neglecting to enforce the Continental System, led to the invasion of Spain in 1808 under Napoleon I, thereby triggering the Peninsular War, with enormous human and property losses, and loss of control over most of the overseas empire.
On February 22 and 23, 1809, a popular insurrection against the French occupation broke out all over Spain.
In March 1812, the Cortes of Cádiz created the first modern Spanish constitution, the Constitution of 1812 (informally named La Pepa).
At the Battle of Vitoria in 1813, an allied army under the Duke of Wellington decisively defeated the French and in 1814 Ferdinand VII was restored as King of Spain.

chapters.narrative: Charles II died in 1700 and was succeeded by his great-nephew Philip, Duke of Anjou, a French prince, and the War of the Spanish Succession (1700–1714) pitted Bourbon against Habsburg proponents [S7]. Fearing Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War, Spain allied with France, invaded Portugal, suffered defeats and ceded Florida in 1763 while gaining Louisiana, later regaining Florida in 1783 [S7]. Spain was at war with Britain 1798–1808, lost a Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar in 1805, and saw colonies emboldened after Britain's defeat in the Río de la Plata invasions of 1806 and 1807 [S7]. Charles IV's failure to enforce the Continental System led to Napoleon's 1808 invasion and the Peninsular War, a 1809 insurrection, the Cortes of Cádiz Constitution of 1812, and Wellington's victory at Vitoria in 1813 restoring Ferdinand VII in 1814 [S7]. These excerpts reflect only a European state-centered viewpoint [S7].

chapters.title: Reign of Isabella II (1833–1868)
chapters.summary: Ferdinand's death in 1833 and the accession of Isabella II sparked the First Carlist War. Isabella was only three years old at the time so her mother, Maria Christina governed as regent.

events.text: The supporters of reform and of limitations on the absolutist rule of the Spanish throne rallied behind Isabella and the regent, Maria Cristina; these reformists were called "Christinos." Though Christino resistance to the insurrection seemed to have been overcome by the end of 1833, Maria Cristina's forces suddenly drove the Carlist armies from most of the Basque country.

Zumalacárregui resuscitated the Carlist cause, and by 1835 had driven the Christino armies to the Ebro River and transformed the Carlist army from a demoralized band into a professional army of 30,000 of superior quality to the government forces.
His 1836 victory at the Battle of Luchana turned the tide of the war, and in 1839, the Convention of Vergara put an end to the first Carlist insurrection.
The Queen Regent preferred to resign and let Espartero become regent instead in 1840.
He was overthrown as regent in 1843 by Ramón María Narváez, a moderate, who was in turn perceived as too reactionary.
Another Carlist uprising, the Matiners' War, was launched in 1846 in Catalonia, but it was poorly organized and suppressed by 1849.
A popular insurrection followed the coup and the Progressive Party obtained widespread support in Spain and came to government in 1854.
After 1856, O'Donnell, who had already marched on Madrid that year and ousted another Espartero ministry, attempted to form the Liberal Union, his own political project.

chapters.narrative: Ferdinand's death in 1833 and the accession of three-year-old Isabella II with Maria Christina as regent sparked the First Carlist War [S8]. Supporters of reform rallied as 'Christinos' and by the end of 1833 drove Carlist armies from most of the Basque country [S8]. Zumalacárregui resuscitated the Carlist cause and by 1835 transformed it into a professional army of 30,000 superior to government forces and drove Christino armies to the Ebro [S8]. His 1836 victory at Luchana turned the tide and the 1839 Convention of Vergara ended the insurrection [S8]. Maria Christina resigned in 1840 for Espartero, overthrown in 1843 by Narváez, while the organized Matiners' War of 1846 was suppressed by 1849 [S8]. A insurrection brought the Progressive Party to government in 1854 before O'Donnell ousted Espartero in 1856 to form the Liberal Union [S8].

chapters.title: Sexenio Democrático (1868–1874)
chapters.summary: In 1868 another insurgency, known as the Glorious Revolution, took place. The progresista generals Francisco Serrano and Juan Prim revolted against Isabella and defeated her moderado generals at the Battle of Alcolea (1868).

events.text: In 1868, Cuba launched a war of independence against Spain.
Two years later, in 1870, the Cortes declared that Spain would again have a king.
The Carlists were the most immediate threat, launching a violent insurrection after their poor showing in the 1872 elections.
The First Spanish Republic (1873–74) was immediately under siege from all quarters.
Following the success of a December 1874 military coup the monarchy was restored in the person of Alfonso XII (the son of former queen Isabella II).

The Restoration period, following the proclamation of the 1876 Constitution, witnessed the installment of an uncompetitive parliamentary system devised by Antonio Cánovas del Castillo, in which two "dynastic" parties, the conservatives and the liberals alternated in control of the government (turnismo).

During the Rif War, the crushing defeat of the Spanish Army in the so-called "Disaster of Annual" in the summer of 1921 brought in a matter of days the catastrophic loss of the lives of about 9,000 Spanish soldiers and the loss of all occupied territory in Morocco that had been gained since 1912.

Preceded by a partial retreat from vulnerable posts in the interior of the protectorate in Morocco, Spain (in joint action with France) turned the tides in Morocco in 1925, and the Abd el-Krim-led Republic of the Rif started to see the beginning of its end after the Alhucemas landing and ensuing seizure of Ajdir, the heart of the Riffian rebellion.
The king fled the country and a republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931.

That same year Cuba launched a war of independence against Spain [S9]. In 1870 the Cortes declared that Spain would again have a king, while the Carlists launched a violent insurrection after their poor showing in the 1872 elections [S9]. The First Spanish Republic (1873–74) was immediately under siege from all quarters [S9]. Following a December 1874 military coup the monarchy was restored in Alfonso XII, the son of Isabella II, and the 1876 Constitution installed an uncompetitive parliamentary system devised by Antonio Cánovas del Castillo with turnismo between conservatives and liberals [S9]. These excerpts reflect only a Spanish-centered viewpoint [S9].

chapters.title: Second Spanish Republic (1931–1936)
chapters.summary: A provisional government presided by Niceto Alcalá Zamora was installed as the Republic, popularly nicknamed as "la niña bonita" ('the pretty girl'), was proclaimed on 14 April 1931, a democratic experiment at a time when democracies were beginning to descend into dictatorships elsewhere in the continent. A Constituent election was called for June 1931.

events.text: A provisional government presided by Niceto Alcalá Zamora was installed as the Republic, popularly nicknamed as "la niña bonita" ('the pretty girl'), was proclaimed on 14 April 1931, a democratic experiment at a time when democracies were beginning to descend into dictatorships elsewhere in the continent.

While the Republican government was able to easily quell the first 1932 coup d'etat led by José Sanjurjo, the generals, who felt humiliated because of the military reform privately developed a strong contempt towards Azaña.
Following the 1933 election, the right-wing Spanish Confederation of the Autonomous Right (CEDA), based on the Catholic vote, was set to enter the radical government.
An armed rising of workers in October 1934, which reached its greatest intensity in Asturias, was forcefully put down.
A devastating 1936–39 civil war was won in 1939 by the rebel forces under Francisco Franco.

chapters.title: Spanish Civil War (1936–39)
chapters.summary: The Spanish Civil War was started by a military coup d'etat in 17–18 July 1936 against the Republican government. The coup, intending to prevent social and economic reforms carried by the new government, had been carefully plotted since the electoral right-wing defeat at the February 1936 election.

events.text: The Spanish Civil War was started by a military coup d'etat in 17–18 July 1936 against the Republican government.

The bombing of Guernica on the afternoon of 26 April 1937 – a mission used as a testing ground for the German Luftwaffe's Condor Legion – was probably the most infamous event of the war and inspired Picasso's painting.
The Battle of the Ebro in July–November 1938 was the final desperate attempt by the Republicans to turn the tide.
After the war, many thousands of Republicans were imprisoned and up to 150,000 were executed between 1939 and 1943.

chapters.narrative: The Spanish Civil War was started by a military coup d'etat in 17-18 July 1936 against the Republican government [S11]. The coup, intending to prevent social and economic reforms carried by the new government, had been carefully plotted since the electoral right-wing defeat at the February 1936 election [S11]. The bombing of Guernica on the afternoon of 26 April 1937 - a mission used as a testing ground for the German Luftwaffe's Condor Legion - was probably the most infamous event of the war and inspired Picasso's painting [S11]. The Battle of the Ebro in July-November 1938 was the final desperate attempt by the Republicans to turn the tide [S11]. After the war, many thousands of Republicans were imprisoned and up to 150,000 were executed between 1939 and 1943 [S11].

chapters.title: Francoist Spain (1939–1975)
chapters.summary: The Francoist regime resulted in the deaths and arrests of hundreds of thousands of people who were either supporters of the previous Second Republic of Spain or potential threats to Franco's state. They were executed, sent to prisons or concentration camps.

events.text: According to Gabriel Jackson, the number of victims of the White Terror (executions and hunger or illness in prisons) between 1939 and 1943 was 200,000.
Though militarily victorious in the 1957–58 Moroccan invasion of Spanish West Africa, Spain gradually relinquished its remaining African colonies.
During the 1960s, Spain began imposing restrictions on Gibraltar, culminating in the closure of the border in 1969.
Spanish Guinea was granted independence as Equatorial Guinea in 1968, while the Moroccan enclave of Ifni had been ceded to Morocco in 1969.
Franco ruled until his death on 20 November 1975, when control was given to King Juan Carlos.
Under its current (1978) constitution, Spain is a constitutional monarchy.
In 1981 the 23-F coup d'état attempt took place.
After earning a sweeping majority at the October 1982 general election, the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) governed the country, with Felipe González as prime minister.

chapters.narrative: The Francoist regime resulted in the deaths and arrests of hundreds of thousands of people who were either supporters of the previous Second Republic of Spain or potential threats to Franco's state, who were executed, sent to prisons or concentration camps [S12]. According to Gabriel Jackson, the number of victims of the White Terror (executions and hunger or illness in prisons) between 1939 and 1943 was 200,000 [S12]. Spain gradually relinquished its remaining African colonies, with Spanish Guinea granted independence as Equatorial Guinea in 1968 while the Moroccan enclave of Ifni was ceded to Morocco in 1969, and during the 1960s Spain began imposing restrictions on Gibraltar culminating in the closure of the border in 1969 [S12]. Franco ruled until his death on 20 November 1975, when control was given to King Juan Carlos [S12].
